excerpt: He was seventeen when he went to war and knew the street talk of Los Angeles. In the dark jungles of Saipan, Guy Gabaldon walked alone into enemy lines and brought back fifteen hundred men without firing a shot. A sharp, unsparing account of courage, the quiet horror of the cliffs, and a Marine who did his job and went home
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
In 1944 on Saipan, Guy Gabaldon brought in fifteen hundred men and civilians. They called him the Pied Piper of Saipan. He was brave and he was smart, but his work was not only the fighting. They recommended him for the Medal of Honor, but they gave him the Navy Cross instead.

He joined the Marines when he was seventeen. He trained at Camp Pendleton and went to the 2nd Regiment of the Second Division. In Los Angeles he had known the first-generation Japanese, and he learned their speech. That was what mattered when he reached the island.

On his first night he went out alone. He used the street Japanese he knew and came back with two prisoners. He walked the jungle in the dark and heard the Japanese planning a big attack. He brought the word back and saved many men.

The war was hard. He saw the civilians jump from the high cliffs into the sea. The women held their children and jumped because they were afraid of the Americans and believed the propaganda. Gabaldon tried to stop them, but they jumped anyway.

Later, at the stockade, he saw a woman he had pulled back from the cliff edge with her child. He looked at her and thought about the war and what it does to people, and he was sad.

They made a movie about him called *Hell to Eternity*, and someone wrote a book called *East L.A. Marine*. But Gabaldon did not talk big. He lived on Saipan with his family for twenty years. He died of a heart attack in Florida on August 31, 2006. He was eighty years old. They took his ashes back to Saipan and scattered them on Mount Tapochau. That was a good place for him.
title: Saipan's Pied Piper
